rows.name: Scratch collaborative project: animate a story
steps: Plan a short story in groups and decide the scenes and which sprite is in each.
Open Scratch and choose sprites and backdrops for the story.
Animate the story with a sequence of blocks, giving each sprite its part.
Use event blocks so that sprites move or change when something happens.
Run the project and fix anything that does not work.
Show the animation to another group.

levels.0: Sprites do nothing when the project is run, or react at the wrong time because no event block starts them.
levels.1: With teammates or the educator, adds an event block to one sprite, though the others are not triggered.
levels.2: Sprites in the story move or change their look when an event such as a key press or click happens.
levels.3: Tests the animation with another group, fixes a sprite that reacted late, and explains which event starts each part.

rows.name: Junior chef – sandwich, salad and one sweet dish
steps: Wash hands, clean the work tables and set out the ingredients.
Make a sandwich, step by step.
Make a salad.
Make one sweet dish.
Arrange the foods on a plate.
Talk about what is on the plate and why.

levels.0: Plate holds one kind of food only, or foods are heaped without any grouping.
levels.1: Once food groups are named by the educator, places foods from two groups on the plate.
levels.2: Plate shows foods from several groups, taken from the sandwich, salad and sweet dish, in sensible amounts.
levels.3: Swaps one food to balance a plate that was heavy in one group and explains the swap.

rows.name: Weave old fabrics to make a rug
steps: Cut old fabrics into long strips and gather them with a frame or base to weave on.
Fix the first set of strips in place.
Weave old fabrics to make a rug by passing the other strips over and under.
Push the rows close together and check the pattern.
Finish the edges and show the rug to the class.

levels.0: Strips are laid side by side or stuck flat, with none going over and under.
levels.1: Starting from rows the educator has begun, weaves a few strips over and under before losing the pattern.
levels.2: Weaves strips over and under following the given pattern for the whole rug, with the pattern holding.
levels.3: Creates a new pattern of their own, weaves it, and explains how the over-under order makes it.

rows.name: Killa making (handwork)
steps: Collect clean recycled materials and talk about what a killa looks like.
Plan the killa on paper.
Make a killa from the materials, building walls and a tower or gate.
Check that it stands and strengthen any weak part.
Display the killa and tell the class how it was made.

levels.0: Recycled pieces are not joined into a structure, and no walls or towers of a killa are visible.
levels.1: Walls of the killa stand only while a partner or educator steadies them, and need extra joining.
levels.2: Killa made from recycled materials stands by itself, with walls and at least one tower or gate.
levels.3: Adds features such as steps or a gate after testing strength, and explains how each part was built.

rows.note: Cell names it only. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Expanded sentences
steps: Write a short sentence on the board.
Ask questions such as what kind, where, when and how to find details to add.
Expand the sentence by adding details.
Children expand their own short sentences in their notebooks.
Read the expanded sentences aloud to a partner.

levels.0: Sentence is copied unchanged, or a word is swapped, with no detail added to it.
levels.1: Adds one detail word after the educator asks 'what kind?' or 'where?'.
levels.2: Rewrites a short sentence with two or more added details, such as how, where or what kind.
levels.3: Expands the same sentence in several ways and explains which details make the picture clearer.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Mental Maths Quiz
steps: Divide the class into teams and explain how the quiz works.
Take part in a mental maths quiz: read each question aloud and ask for answers without writing.
Allow a short time for each answer.
Check the answers and keep score for each team.
Talk about the quick ways children used to get answers.

levels.0: Answers come only after counting on fingers or drawing, or many are incorrect or skipped.
levels.1: Answers some questions quickly when numbers are small, but needs extra time or a hint for others.
levels.2: Gives most answers aloud quickly and correctly without counting aids or writing.
levels.3: Explains the quick method used for an answer and solves a harder question in the same time.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Write an alternative story ending
steps: Read The Abominable Snowman and Yoshi the Stonecutter and talk about how each one ends.
Ask what else might have happened at the end.
Plan a different ending in a few words.
Write an alternative ending.
Read the ending to a partner and compare endings.

levels.0: Writing repeats the original ending, or the ending does not follow from the tale.
levels.1: With a what-if question from the educator, writes one sentence of a different ending.
levels.2: Writes a different ending that follows on from the tale and differs from the original.
levels.3: Compares the new ending with the original and explains how the characters' fate changes.

rows.note: LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Write a circular story
steps: Talk about stories that end where they began.
Plan a circular story by deciding on the opening and how the ending will return to it.
Write a circular story.
Read the beginning and ending to a partner to check they match up.
Share a few circular stories with the class.

levels.0: Story ends somewhere new, with the opening scene or sentence never coming back.
levels.1: Only after being shown the opening line does the ending echo it.
levels.2: Story's final lines return to the opening event or sentence, so it loops back to the start.
levels.3: Tells the circular story aloud and explains in own words why the ending leads back to the beginning.

rows.note: LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Perform in character
steps: Listen carefully to character voice as the educator reads part of a story.
Talk about how the voice changes for different characters.
Perform in character using the voice in different ways.
Talk about the sequence of the story.
Watch other groups and say which voice suited each character.

levels.0: Performance uses one flat voice throughout, and the order of events is jumbled or missing.
levels.1: Cues from a partner help the character's voice change a little, and the events come in order with pauses.
levels.2: Acts out the story in a character voice, changing it for different moments, with events in order.
levels.3: Switches characters in a retelling, with a distinct voice for each, and says why the voice changes.

rows.name: Hindi: कविता चार्ट पेपर पर लिखना, चित्र निर्माण (जाड़े की धूप)
steps: कविता 'जाड़े की धूप' पढ़ें।
कविता को चार्ट पेपर पर लिखें।
चित्र बनाएँ।
जाड़े की धूप के बारे में अपनी कुछ पंक्तियाँ लिखें।
चार्ट कक्षा में दिखाएँ और कविता सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Chart holds a copied poem or a few words, with no lines of their own about winter sunshine.
levels.1: With the educator's first line, adds one or two lines about sunshine in winter and a drawing.
levels.2: Writes a short poem of their own on the chart paper about winter sunshine, with a matching picture.
levels.3: Poem uses a comparison or a feeling about the warmth of the sun and is read aloud with expression.

rows.name: Hindi: विचार-अभिव्यक्ति, कहानी-पठन, अनुच्छेद-लेखन (अब हम दोस्त हैं)
steps: बच्चे दोस्ती के बारे में अपने विचार व्यक्त करें।
कहानी 'अब हम दोस्त हैं' पढ़ें और सुनाएँ।
कहानी के बारे में साथी से बात करें।
अनुच्छेद-लेखन करें।
अनुच्छेद पढ़कर सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Paragraph is one or two disconnected words or sentences copied from the book, with no ideas of their own on friendship.
levels.1: After talking with a partner, writes one or two sentences about friendship, needing help to join them into a paragraph.
levels.2: Writes a paragraph of several sentences in own words about the story and about friendship.
levels.3: Paragraph links the story to a real friendship, giving a reason, and is read out to the group.

rows.name: Hindi: अनुच्छेद-लेखन, सूची-निर्माण, रंग भरकर रंगों के नाम (जैसी हूँ मैं)
steps: कहानी 'जैसी हूँ मैं अच्छी हूँ' पढ़ें।
अनुच्छेद लिखें।
सूची बनाएँ।
रंग भरकर रंगों के नाम लिखें।
साथी को अपना लिखा सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Coloured picture has labels only, or copied sentences, and nothing of their own about it.
levels.1: Asked 'what do you see?' by the educator, writes one sentence about the picture.
levels.2: Sentences of own about the coloured picture appear, using colour names written in Hindi.
levels.3: Describes the picture with a reason for the colours chosen and reads the paragraph to a partner.

rows.name: Paper strip weaving, cardboard loom, classroom weaving wall
steps: Cut paper strips in two colours and show the over-under technique by weaving one strip through a few others.
Children practise weaving paper strips over and under, copying a given pattern card.
Each child makes a cardboard loom by cutting evenly spaced slits along two edges of a piece of cardboard.
Children weave their paper strips through the loom, following the pattern.
Join the woven pieces together to build a classroom weaving wall.
Walk along the wall and let children say which pattern they wove and check that each row alternates.

levels.0: Strips are laid side by side or stacked, with no alternating over-under crossings visible anywhere in the weave.
levels.1: Once an educator starts the first row or a partner steadies the loom, strips alternate over and under for a few crossings.
levels.2: Strips alternate over and under across whole rows and match the given pattern card, with at most one slip.
levels.3: Weaves a new pattern of their own or extends the card pattern, and explains aloud how each row starts to alternate.

rows.name: Studying artworks of Paul Klee and Yayoi Kusama
steps: Show pictures of artworks by Paul Klee and Yayoi Kusama where every child can see them.
Children look quietly for a minute, then point to lines and patterns they notice.
In a circle, each child describes one line or pattern using words such as wavy, straight, spotted or repeating.
Compare the two artists' work and talk about what is similar and what is different.
Each child chooses one artwork and says one sentence about its lines or patterns to a partner.

levels.0: Comments name the picture's subject or colour only, with no mention of any line or pattern.
levels.1: After educator prompts such as 'What repeats here?', names one line or pattern, pointing to it in the picture.
levels.2: Unprompted, describes at least two lines or patterns in an artwork, using words such as wavy, straight, spotted or repeating.
levels.3: Compares lines and patterns across the two artists' works, saying how they differ and giving a reason for a favourite.

rows.name: Doodle & Describe
steps: Give each child a blank page and a couple of minutes to doodle freely.
Children look at their doodle and think of words for its shapes, lines and colours.
Each child writes sentences of their own describing the doodle.
Partners swap pages; the reader points to each part of the doodle the sentences describe.
A few children read their description aloud and the class guesses what the doodle looks like.

levels.0: Doodle has only a title or single words beside it, with no complete sentence describing what is drawn.
levels.1: With an educator asking 'What do you see?' and helping to sound out words, one sentence about the doodle is written.
levels.2: Writes two or more complete sentences in own words that match features of the doodle, with capital letters and full stops.
levels.3: Writes sentences with added detail such as position, size or number, and a partner can find each described feature in the doodle.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Expanded Sentences
steps: Write a short sentence on the board and read it aloud with the class.
Ask who, what kind, where and when questions, and add the answers to the sentence one detail at a time.
In pairs, children expand a short sentence orally.
Each child writes their own short sentence, then writes it again with at least two added details.
Read the short and expanded versions aloud and compare how they differ.

levels.0: Rewrites the short sentence unchanged or adds only an unrelated word, so the sentence stays the same length.
levels.1: Adds one detail, such as a colour or a place, only after the educator asks 'Where?' or 'What kind?'.
levels.2: Expands a short sentence alone by adding two or more details, such as describing words and where or when, that still read correctly.
levels.3: Builds the same sentence up in several steps with growing detail, and tells a partner what each added word tells the reader.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Short Essay + Drawing
steps: Choose a familiar topic with the class and talk about it for a few minutes.
Each child draws a picture of the topic and jots down three ideas in the order they want to write them.
Children write a short essay with an opening idea, a middle idea and a closing idea.
Partners read each other's essays and check that the ideas follow the order of the drawing.
Display the essays with their drawings and let children read one aloud.

levels.0: Sentences jump between ideas or repeat one idea, with no clear first, next or last point in the essay.
levels.1: Using a planning frame with first, next and last boxes, ideas sit in order but one part is thin or missing.
levels.2: Short essay has an opening idea, one or two middle ideas and a closing idea in a sensible order matching the drawing.
levels.3: Uses linking words such as first, then and finally, and explains to a partner why the ideas were placed in that order.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Design a robot with labels
steps: Read about robots (The Pepper robot, What is a Drone?, Flying a drone) and talk about what each one can do.
Children draw a large design of their own robot on paper.
Add labels with lines pointing to the robot's parts, saying what each part does.
Write short headings and sentences that sort the information about the robot under each heading.
Partners read each other's design and say what the robot looks like and can do.

levels.0: Drawing shows a robot with no labels or headings, or labels sit in one unsorted list under no heading.
levels.1: Given a heading idea by the educator, writes one heading with a sentence or labels under it, leaving other parts unsorted.
levels.2: Writes information about their own robot under two or more clear headings, with labelled parts that match the drawing.
levels.3: Chooses own headings that fit the information and adds facts from the robot reading, explaining why each heading was chosen.

rows.name: Write instructions for a robot
steps: Look at an example set of instructions and underline the first word of each step, talking about command words such as 'walk' and 'turn'.
Choose a simple task for a robot to do.
Children write numbered steps for the robot, starting each step with a command verb.
A partner acts as the robot and follows the steps exactly as written.
Children fix any step that did not work and read the final instructions to the class.

levels.0: Steps begin with words like 'The robot' or 'Then', so no step opens with a command verb such as 'walk' or 'turn'.
levels.1: Reminded to start with an action word, two or three steps open with command verbs while other steps do not.
levels.2: Every step in the numbered set starts with a command verb and the steps run in a workable order.
levels.3: Revises steps after a partner acting as the robot follows them exactly, keeping a precise command verb at the start of each.

rows.name: Write a robot explanation text
steps: Recap what the class learned about robots and list key facts on the board.
Each child chooses a robot and decides on two or three headings for their text.
Children write an explanation under each heading about what the robot is, how it works or what it is for.
Partners find each heading in the text and say whether the sentences below it fit.
Share a few explanation texts with the class.

levels.0: Explanation runs as one block of text with no headings, or headings are present but the sentences below do not match them.
levels.1: Supplied with heading ideas by the educator, writes sentences under one heading while the rest stays a single run of text.
levels.2: Explanation about a robot is split by two or more headings, and the sentences under each heading match it.
levels.3: Adds an extra heading of their own and fits new facts beneath it, so a partner can find any fact quickly using the headings.

rows.name: Present ideas about a robot
steps: Each child prepares a few notes or a picture about a robot.
Children practise saying their ideas to a partner.
In small groups, each child presents their ideas about a robot, using the notes or picture.
Group members listen to the ideas of others and each listener says one thing they learned.
Educator notes whether each presenter was heard clearly and used the notes or picture.

levels.0: Stands before the group but reads notes silently or says nothing, so the group hears no ideas about the robot.
levels.1: Standing beside an educator or partner who prompts each point, shares one or two ideas in a quiet voice from the notes.
levels.2: Speaks to the group for several sentences about the robot, pointing to notes or picture, and each idea is audible.
levels.3: Answers a listener's question about the robot and adds an idea that is not on the notes, linking it to the picture.

rows.name: Perform a poem in a group
steps: Read the poem the group has chosen from Busy Day, Downhill Racer or The River.
Each group decides who reads which lines and where all voices join.
Practise the poem, deciding which words to say loudly, softly, quickly or slowly.
Groups perform the poem for the class while the others listen to the reading aloud.
After each performance, children say in the group what they liked and give an opinion on what to change.

levels.0: Poem is read in an even, flat voice, with lines run together and no change in volume or pace.
levels.1: Reciting alongside a partner or with educator cues, voice changes on one or two lines while other lines stay flat.
levels.2: Recites the poem with clear changes in loudness or speed that match the words, and joins the group on time.
levels.3: Gives reasons for chosen voice changes, such as soft for a calm line, and recites with changes that fit each part.

rows.name: Write a shape poem
steps: Read a model poem together and notice the rhyming words.
Each child chooses a shape and lists words that describe it.
Find rhyming word pairs from the list.
Write the poem so that the lines are arranged in the chosen shape.
Read the shape poem aloud to a partner, who points out the rhymes.

levels.0: Lines are written without rhyming pairs, or the poem copies the model line for line with no new words.
levels.1: Following the model line by line with educator help, one rhyming pair appears while other lines do not rhyme.
levels.2: Short poem written in the chosen shape has at least two rhyming pairs and follows the pattern of the model.
levels.3: Poem on a self-chosen shape uses rhymes not found in the model, and is read aloud with the rhyming words stressed.

rows.name: Write a poem with a repeating pattern
steps: Read a model poem that has a repeating line or pattern and clap the repeat together.
Each child chooses a topic and a line to repeat.
Write the poem using the repeated line and new lines that rhyme.
Read the poems aloud while the class joins in on the repeating line.
Partners check that the repeating line appears in each place it should.

levels.0: Poem lines are all different, with no repeated line or rhyme appearing anywhere in the writing.
levels.1: Using a sentence starter from the educator, repeats a line twice, but the new lines do not rhyme.
levels.2: Poem repeats a chosen line at set places and has rhyming words in at least two of the new lines.
levels.3: Changes the repeating line slightly to fit each verse while keeping rhymes, and says in own words what the repeat adds.

rows.name: Find the centre of a circle by folding
steps: Give each child a paper circle and show how to fold it in half and in half again.
Open the circle; the crease lines meet at the centre, which children mark.
Draw a pointer arrow from the centre, then call out a quarter turn, half turn or full turn for children to turn the pointer using the folds.
In pairs, one child calls a turn and the other turns the pointer and checks it against the creases.
Share which turns were easy and how the folds helped.

levels.0: Pointer turns by an arbitrary amount, so it does not stop on the fold lines for a quarter, half or full turn.
levels.1: Turns correctly for a half or full turn but needs the educator to show the quarter turn along the folds.
levels.2: Pointer turns through a quarter, half and full turn as called, stopping on the matching crease each time.
levels.3: Predicts where the pointer will stop for a new turn, such as two quarter turns one after the other, and shows it with the folds.

rows.name: Chance experiments
steps: Choose a chance activity with the class, such as rolling a die or drawing from a bag.
Before trying it, children list every possible outcome.
Try the activity several times and record each result with tally marks.
Present the results as a tally or chart and describe which outcome came up most.
Predict the more likely outcome for the next few tries and test it.

levels.0: Outcomes are not listed before trying, and the stated prediction ignores the tally marks recorded.
levels.1: Asked what could happen, lists some outcomes and names the most frequent result while pointing to the tally.
levels.2: Lists every possible outcome before trying, then predicts the more likely one after several trials, pointing to the highest tally.
levels.3: Explains from own tally why one outcome came up more, and predicts what a further set of trials would show.

rows.name: Project: 100 Squares
steps: Give each child a hundred square grid to use for the 100 Squares project.
Children choose a number pattern and mark it on the grid.
Write the first few terms of the pattern, then continue it for three more terms.
A partner checks the new terms by looking at the marked squares.
Share what the class noticed about the patterns on the grid.

levels.0: Next numbers written after the given terms do not follow the step between them, jumping by differing amounts.
levels.1: Pointing along the hundred square or helped by a partner's hint, continues the pattern for one or two terms only.
levels.2: Writes three more terms after the first few given, each following the same step, and marks them on the grid.
levels.3: Names the rule of the pattern in own words and continues it past three terms, or creates a new pattern for a partner.

rows.note: Cell names it only. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Hindi: होली की कहानी, चित्र में रंग भरना, शब्द-पहेली, कविता-लेखन
steps: होली की कहानी पढ़ें।
कहानी के बारे में बात करें कि उसमें क्या-क्या हुआ।
चित्र में रंग भरें।
शब्द-पहेली हल करें।
कहानी से जुड़े प्रश्नों के उत्तर पूरे वाक्यों में लिखें।
कविता-लेखन करें और एक-दो बच्चे अपनी रचना पढ़कर सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Answers to Holi story questions are single words or copied phrases, with no complete sentence written.
levels.1: Hearing each question read aloud and given the first word by the educator, writes some answers as full sentences.
levels.2: Writes answers to the story questions in full Hindi sentences of their own, each with a verb and ending in '।'.
levels.3: Answers go beyond the text, adding a reason or an opinion about the Holi story, still in full sentences.

rows.name: Hindi: श्रुतलेखन (dictation)
steps: बच्चे कॉपी और पेंसिल निकालकर तैयार हों।
एक वाक्य दो बार धीरे-धीरे बोलें।
श्रुतलेखन करें: बच्चे सुनकर वाक्य अपनी कॉपी में लिखें।
बच्चे साथी से कॉपी बदलकर वाक्य की वर्तनी जाँचें।
गलत लिखे शब्दों को सही वर्तनी में दोबारा लिखें।

levels.0: Dictated sentence has several words with missing or wrong matras ('मात्रा'), so many words cannot be read as dictated.
levels.1: After the sentence is repeated word by word, most words are written, though two or three show wrong matras.
levels.2: Dictated sentence is written with every word spelt correctly, including matras, and ends with '।'.
levels.3: Writes a longer dictated sentence correctly and corrects a partner's misspelt word, saying which matra was wrong.

rows.note: Routine. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Micro:bit project
steps: Give each pair a micro:bit and recall together what was done in the last session.
Children choose a pattern to show on the LED display and draw it on paper.
Program the micro:bit so the pattern appears when an input is pressed.
Send the program to the micro:bit and test by pressing the input.
Fix anything that did not work, then show the result to another pair.

levels.0: Micro:bit LEDs stay blank or show a pattern from the start, with no response when a button is pressed.
levels.1: With a partner or educator pointing to the right block, a pattern appears on the LEDs but is not tied to the press.
levels.2: Pressing a button makes the LEDs show the chosen pattern, matching the one drawn in the plan.
levels.3: Programs different patterns for two different inputs and explains which block links each button to its pattern.

rows.name: Preservatives: making pickles and papads
steps: Talk about natural and artificial preservatives, and let children share foods they know that keep for a long time.
Wash hands and set out the materials for pickles and papads.
Make pickles and papads in groups, noting what is done to help them keep.
Children say why they think the pickles and papads will not spoil quickly.
Each child names one way to keep food from spoiling.

levels.0: Answers about keeping food fresh name no method, saying only that food 'goes bad' without naming how to stop it.
levels.1: Seeing the pickles and papads, names one ingredient or step used in making them once the educator points to it.
levels.2: Names at least one way to keep food from spoiling, such as a preservative used in the pickles or papads.
levels.3: Names two ways, sorting them as natural or artificial, and says in own words why preserved food lasts longer.

rows.name: Fabric weaving on a cardboard loom
steps: Prepare the cardboard loom with yarn threads stretched across it.
Practise fabric weaving by passing yarn over and under the threads on the loom.
Keep weaving row after row, packing the rows together, until the piece is complete.
Tie off the ends so the woven piece makes a final product.
Show the finished piece to the group and say how it was woven.

levels.0: Yarn is pulled across the loom without alternating, leaving loose loops and no finished woven piece.
levels.1: Helped by an educator who starts each row, yarn alternates over and under for part of the loom and the piece stays unfinished.
levels.2: Yarn alternates over and under in every row on the loom, and a finished woven piece with tied-off ends is shown.
levels.3: Finished piece shows a pattern of own planning, such as colour stripes, and the weaver explains how the over-under rows were built.

rows.name: Republic Day song practice
steps: Gather the class and listen to the Republic Day song once.
Practise the song line by line, with children echoing each line.
Sing the whole song together at a steady pace.
Small groups take turns singing the song for the others.
Children say which part they sing best and which part to practise more.

levels.0: Mouths or hums only, or sings lines with words and tune out of step with the group.
levels.1: Joins in on the chorus or some lines when the educator leads, and drops out between them.
levels.2: Sings the song's words along with the group from start to end, keeping to the same tune and pace.
levels.3: Sings with steady tune and clear words, and leads a line or helps others keep time when asked.

rows.note: LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Mass: use kg and grams, scale reading, estimate mass
steps: Show kilograms and grams on the scale and talk about when each unit is used.
Children practise reading the scale for a few objects.
Before weighing, each child estimates the mass of a familiar object and writes it down.
Weigh the object, record the reading in kg or g, and compare it with the estimate.
Share how close the estimates were and what helped.

levels.0: Estimates are given without a unit, or the scale reading is written without kg or g, so the check cannot be compared.
levels.1: Reads the mass with the educator pointing to the scale marks, but estimates are far from the weighed value.
levels.2: Estimates the mass of an object in g or kg, weighs it, and records both readings with correct units.
levels.3: Estimates land close to the weighed values with a sensible choice of g or kg, and a reason from a known object is given.

rows.name: Grain to Flour: from wheat to ladoo
steps: Find out where flour comes from by looking at wheat grains together.
Experience the traditional method of making flour, with the educator handling anything unsafe.
Sort real or pictured foods into grains and pulses.
Make ladoo together in groups.
Children say which foods in the day's work were grains and which were pulses.

levels.0: Foods are placed in mixed groups, with grains and pulses side by side and no stated reason for the grouping.
levels.1: Sorts a few samples correctly after the educator names one grain and one pulse as examples, leaving others misplaced.
levels.2: Sorts real or pictured foods into grains and pulses, with wheat among the grains, and no more than one misplaced.
levels.3: Adds a food of their own to each group after sorting every sample, and says how a grain differs from a pulse.

rows.note: Taken from the Dec 2025 row text; 'Making ladoo' from the heading only. LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Design a snowman with socks and buttons
steps: Look at the socks and buttons and talk about what a snowman needs.
Each child draws a plan to design their snowman.
Shape the snowman's body from a sock.
Attach the buttons and other parts using the stitching technique taught.
Show the finished snowman and compare it with the plan.

levels.0: Snowman is left as a sock with buttons loose or stuck on, with no stitches holding any part.
levels.1: Threading help from an educator gets one or two buttons stitched on, and the product stays unfinished.
levels.2: Finished snowman has buttons attached with stitches and the sock shaped as designed, matching the plan drawing.
levels.3: Finished snowman adds own sewn features, and the maker names the stitch used and what could improve.

rows.note: LO link added in second pass (nearest same-grade LO or new LO).

rows.name: Colour wheel; warm and cool colours
steps: Draw a large circle on paper and divide it into equal segments.
Make a colour wheel by colouring the primary colours first, then the secondary colours.
Label each colour with its name.
Work with warm and cool colours by marking or grouping the wheel's colours as warm or cool.
Share the wheels and say which colours felt warm and which felt cool.

levels.0: Colour wheel has colours in no consistent order, and labels are missing or primary and secondary are not told apart.
levels.1: Using the educator's finished wheel as a guide, names the primary colours but secondary labels are partly missing.
levels.2: Painted wheel has primary and secondary colours named correctly, with warm and cool colours grouped.
levels.3: Sorts a new colour into warm or cool and names which two primary colours mix to make a chosen secondary colour.

rows.name: Hindi: भालू का घर – कहानी का अंत बदलना, पशु-पक्षियों के घर
steps: कहानी-वाचन करें।
कहानी के अंत के बारे में बात करें कि अंत में क्या हुआ।

levels.1: After talking through a new ending with the educator, writes one sentence for it, in words close to the story's.

rows.name: Write an ending to a given story
steps: Read the given story together and stop before the ending.
Talk about how it could end and what might happen next.
Each child plans a new ending in a few words.
Children write the ending to the story in their own sentences.
Read the ending aloud to a partner and compare how the endings differ.

levels.0: Ending is left blank, or retells the story's own ending in the same words with nothing new.
levels.1: Following the educator's 'What if...?' question, writes a one-sentence different ending not connected to earlier events.
levels.2: Writes an ending different from the original that follows from earlier events, in at least two sentences.
levels.3: Compares own ending with the original, saying what changes for the characters, and the ending keeps the tale's style.

rows.name: Write a short animal story with a beginning, middle and end
steps: Talk about animals and choose one for a story, with a problem it could face.
Fold paper into three parts for the beginning, middle and end, and jot ideas in each.
Write a short animal story with a clear beginning, middle and end.
Read the story to a partner, who points to where each part starts.
Share a few stories with the class.

levels.0: Story is a single event or list of facts about an animal, with no separate beginning, middle and end.
levels.1: With a three-part folded plan from the educator, two parts are written, usually beginning and middle, with no clear end.
levels.2: Animal story has a clear beginning that introduces the animal, a middle event, and an ending that closes it.
levels.3: Story's ending resolves the problem set up in the beginning, and the writer points out each part to a partner.

rows.name: Project – Sorting Orange Juice
steps: Introduce the Sorting Orange Juice project and read its problem together.
Children underline the numbers and what is being asked.
Children work out the problem in two steps, writing each step as a number sentence.
Check the answer by reading it back against the problem.
Pairs explain their two steps to another pair.

levels.0: Work shows one number operation that answers only part of the problem, and the final answer does not address the question asked.
levels.1: Guided by the educator splitting the problem into parts, the first step is worked correctly but the second is missing or mistaken.
levels.2: Two steps are written as number sentences in the right order, and the final answer is labelled and fits the situation.
levels.3: Explains why each step is needed, checks the answer against the story, and makes up a similar two-step problem.

rows.name: Hindi: पौधारोपण गतिविधि, सूचना-लेखन, जानवरों के नाम
steps: पौधारोपण करें।
पौधा लगाते समय बात करें कि प्रकृति को बचाने के लिए हम क्या कर सकते हैं।
सूचना-लेखन करें: प्रकृति की रक्षा के बारे में छोटी सूचना अपने वाक्यों में लिखें।
जानवरों के नाम बताएँ।
साथी को अपनी सूचना पढ़कर सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Writing is a list of words or a copied line, with no notice heading 'सूचना' and no message about nature.
levels.1: Copying a model notice and using the educator's sentence starter, writes a heading and one sentence about caring for nature.
levels.2: Notice has a heading 'सूचना' and two or more sentences in own words telling others how to protect nature.
levels.3: Notice gives a reason for protecting nature and a clear request to readers, all in own sentences.

rows.name: Hindi: होली के रंग – कविता-लेखन
steps: होली की कहानी पढ़ें।
कहानी के बारे में बात करें कि उसमें क्या-क्या हुआ।
कहानी से जुड़े प्रश्नों के उत्तर पूरे वाक्यों में लिखें।
कविता-लेखन करें: होली पर अपनी कविता लिखें।
कविता साथी या कक्षा को सुनाएँ।

levels.0: Lines about Holi are single words or phrases, so no sentence in the notebook answers a question about the story.
levels.1: When the educator asks each question aloud and a partner helps, one sentence about the story is written.
levels.2: Notebook answers on the Holi story are full sentences, and poem lines reuse events or words from the story.
levels.3: Poem lines and answers together show own ideas beyond the text, such as feelings about the festival, in complete sentences.

rows.name: Light experiment project
steps: Set up a place that is dim enough for a light source to show clearly.
Each group chooses an object and places it between the light source and a wall or sheet of paper.
Children make a shadow with the object and observe it.
Draw the shadow and write or say what is needed to make it.
Share the drawings and talk about what changed the shadow.

levels.0: Light source is switched on but the object is not between it and the surface, so no shadow appears.
levels.1: Held steady by an educator, the light source casts a shadow of the object, and the maker points to it.
levels.2: Object placed in the light's path makes a clear shadow on a surface, which is pointed out and named.
levels.3: Moves the object or light to change the shadow's size or position, and says what was changed and what happened.

rows.name: Create your own Smart Bedroom
steps: Talk about what a smart bedroom could do on its own.
Each child plans one feature on paper and draws the LED pattern that shows it.
Program the micro:bit so that pressing an input shows the pattern on the LEDs.
Test the program with the drawn bedroom and fix any problems.
Show the Smart Bedroom to the group and say what the pattern means.

levels.0: Smart bedroom plan lists ideas, but the micro:bit shows nothing, or a pattern shows without any press.
levels.1: Once a partner finds the input block, the bedroom feature shows an LED pattern for a button, though it sometimes fails.
levels.2: Pressing the chosen input makes the LEDs show the pattern that stands for the bedroom feature, every time it is tested.
levels.3: Adds a second input and pattern for another feature, and tells viewers what each press stands for.

rows.name: Baking in an oven or on a stove
steps: Look at the raw dough together and note its texture, colour and smell.
Bake the dough in an oven or on a stove, with only the educator handling the heat.
Observe how the raw dough changes into bread or cake when heated.
Talk about texture, colour, smell and taste before and after baking.
Each child names the cooking method used and says what it did to the dough.

levels.0: Remarks describe the dough only, with no cooking method named and no change after heating mentioned.
levels.1: When asked by the educator, names the cooking method but describes the change with one vague word.
levels.2: Names baking or the method used and states one change seen, such as in texture or colour.
levels.3: Compares before and after on texture, colour, smell and taste, and links each change to the heat of cooking.

rows.name: Steam in a pan
steps: Heat water in a pan with only the educator handling the heat, while children stand back.
Observe the water turning into steam.
Explain that steam is hot water vapour.
Discuss safety rules while observing steam.
Relate steam to daily life, such as cooking rice, vegetables and idlis, and let each child name a food cooked with steam.

levels.0: Statements about the pan mention only the water or noise, with no steam, cooking method or effect on food named.
levels.1: Prompted by the educator's picture of idlis or rice, names steaming but says little about what steam does.
levels.2: Names steaming as a cooking method and says that steam, hot water vapour, cooks food such as rice or idlis.
levels.3: Describes the water changing to steam in the pan, links it to steaming food, and states one safety rule.

rows.name: Nail string art
steps: Before the lesson, fix nails in a simple outline on a board so each child or pair has a surface to wrap around.
Show how to tie a string to one nail and wrap it round other nails to make straight lines.
Children create patterns by wrapping colourful strings around nails, changing to a second colour at least once.
Children show their pattern to a partner and name the shape and colours they used.

levels.0: Wrapping stays on one nail or tangles, so no clear design shows and only a single colour of string is used.
levels.1: Once the educator ties the first knot, a design appears in two colours but gaps remain between wraps.
levels.2: Strings wrapped nail to nail form a recognisable star, flower or letter shape using two or more colours.
levels.3: Designs a new shape on the nails unprompted, changes colours deliberately, and explains why each colour sits where it does.

rows.name: Texture drawing through shading
steps: Gather or point out objects in the room with different surfaces, and let children touch them and say how each feels.
Show on the board how lines and shading can make a surface look rough, smooth or bumpy.
Children draw texture through shading, choosing one surface and using pencil lines and shading to show how it would feel.
Partners look at each drawing and guess how the surface would feel, then say which marks told them.

levels.0: Page shows outlines only, with flat or even shading that does not suggest rough, smooth or bumpy.
levels.1: After the educator shows a sample, short dashes or a patch of shading appear, though two textures look alike.
levels.2: Lines and shading change across the drawing so a partner can tell if the surface looks rough, smooth or bumpy.
levels.3: Several different textures are drawn with varied pressure and line types, and the artist explains which marks make each feel different.

rows.name: Artist focus – Henri Rousseau Jungle
steps: Display Henri Rousseau's jungle art where every child can see it.
Children look quietly for a minute and point to what seems nearest to them and what seems farthest away.
In the circle, children describe the layers they can see, using words such as front, middle and back.
Each child shares one layer they noticed with a partner, who says whether they see it too.

levels.0: Names single objects in the picture, such as a leaf or animal, without saying which are in front or behind.
levels.1: Prompted by the educator's 'what is at the front?', one front item and one back item are named.
levels.2: Describes at least two layers, such as plants in front and trees behind, using words like front, middle and back.
levels.3: Compares layers in the jungle picture with another nature scene and says how overlapping shapes make depth.

rows.name: Write structured paragraphs
steps: Choose an underwater topic from the unit and gather a few facts about it on the board with the class.
Show a frame of topic sentence, details and conclusion, and model one paragraph on the board with a heading.
Children write paragraphs with a topic sentence, details and conclusion on a topic they pick, adding a heading.
Partners read each other's paragraph and tick the topic sentence, the details and the conclusion.

levels.0: Writing is a list of loose sentences with no opening statement, closing line or heading.
levels.1: Using the educator's sentence frame, a topic sentence and one or two details appear, but ending and heading are missing.
levels.2: Paragraph under a heading opens with a topic sentence, adds details about the same topic, and ends with a concluding line.
levels.3: Writes a paragraph on a fresh topic with its own heading and explains what each of the three parts does.

rows.name: Create information charts (2–3 columns)
steps: Collect facts about underwater life on the board as children call them out.
Draw a chart with 2 or 3 columns on the board and show how each column gets a heading.
Children create an information chart with 2–3 columns, writing facts under the right heading.
Partners swap charts and check that each fact sits under the heading it belongs to.

levels.0: Facts are scattered across the page with no column lines or headings, or one heading is used for everything.
levels.1: Given a ruled template, headings are copied in and a few facts fill one or two columns.
levels.2: A chart of two or three columns, each with a heading, holds facts that match the heading above them.
levels.3: Plans own column headings for a new topic and fills the chart, then explains why each fact belongs in its column.

rows.name: Explain food chains orally; share coral reef facts
steps: Give children time to prepare a picture or a few notes about a food chain or a coral reef fact.
In the circle, children explain food chains orally, pointing to their picture or notes.
Children share coral reef facts with the group.
Take part in guided report discussions, with the educator asking a question and a listener asking one too.

levels.0: Speaks only a word or two, or stays silent, and the group cannot tell what was found out.
levels.1: Prompts such as 'what eats what?' lead to one food chain link, read from the notes.
levels.2: Presents a food chain or reef fact to the group in connected sentences, glancing at notes or pointing to a picture.
levels.3: Presents clearly without reading, answers a listener's question, and adds a fact that is not on the notes.

rows.name: Write rhyming verses, a short ode and a class poem
steps: Read a short rhyming model poem aloud and have children spot and underline the rhyming words.
Children list rhyming pairs for a creature of their choice and write rhyming verses.
Children compose a short ode of 2–3 stanzas using their rhyming pairs.
Each child contributes a line to a class poem, and the class reads the finished poem aloud together.

levels.0: Lines are written without end rhyme, or copy the model line for line.
levels.1: Helped by a rhyme word list, one rhyming pair appears but the other lines do not match.
levels.2: Short poem following the model has line endings that rhyme in each verse, in the shape of the model.
levels.3: Poem on own creature uses fresh rhyming pairs not found in the model, and the poet says how the rhymes were found.

rows.name: Recite poems clearly and confidently
steps: Choose a poem and read it aloud once as a model, using your voice and face to show feeling.
Children recite the poem clearly in pairs, with the partner listening for words that are hard to hear.
Practise projection and pacing by reciting to the far side of the room and pausing at line ends.
Children express emotion through voice and facial expression as each recites to the class, and listeners name one thing done well.

levels.0: Poem is mumbled or read in one flat tone, with words skipped and little change in face.
levels.1: Echoing the educator line by line, words are clear but expression changes in only a line or two.
levels.2: Poem is said audibly at an even pace, with voice and face matching the feeling of the lines.
levels.3: Recites from memory with deliberate pauses and varied voice, and also says a tongue twister without stumbling after practice.

rows.name: Project: Possibly odd
steps: Open the project 'Possibly odd' (unit 1) and read what it asks together so every child knows the task.
Give children the numbers or materials the project uses, and have them sort numbers up to 100 into odd and even.
Children record their sorted numbers and write how they decided where each one goes.
Partners compare their lists and talk about any number they placed differently.

levels.0: Numbers are placed in odd and even groups with no pattern, or the ones digit is not used.
levels.1: Pairing counters or following a hint, a few numbers are sorted correctly while larger ones are misplaced.
levels.2: Numbers up to 100 are sorted into odd and even lists, with the ones digit named as the reason.
levels.3: Predicts whether a number chosen by a partner is odd or even and justifies it using its ones digit.

steps: Open the project 'Strange submarines' (unit 3) and read the task aloud with the class.
Ask children to say in their own words what the problem asks before they start.
Children work through the project, writing each step of the working on paper.
Pairs compare working and answers and explain how each step led to the next.

levels.0: Working shows one operation only, or numbers from the problem are combined without reading what is asked.
levels.1: Reading the problem aloud with the educator, one step is worked and the second is left.
levels.2: Both steps of the submarine problem are written as number sentences and the final answer fits the question.
levels.3: Makes up an own two-step problem on a similar theme and explains how each step leads to the answer.

rows.name: Project: Borrowing pencil
steps: Open the project 'Borrowing pencil' (unit 5) and read the task aloud with the class.
Ask children to say in their own words what the problem asks before they start.
Children work through the project, writing each step of the working on paper.
Pairs compare working and answers and explain how each step led to the next.

levels.0: Answer is a single number with no steps visible, and it does not match what the pencil problem asks.
levels.1: After a partner re-reads the problem, one calculation is shown and the second step is unfinished.
levels.2: Two linked calculations appear in the working, and the answer is written as a sentence that answers the question.
levels.3: Changes the numbers or story of the pencil problem and solves the new two-step version, explaining the order of steps.

rows.name: Project: Time a task
steps: Open the project 'Time a task' (unit 4) and read what it asks together.
Choose a short classroom task, and have children note the start time from a clock before beginning.
Children do the task, note the end time, and work out how long it took.
Children share their start time, end time and length with a partner and check each other's working.

levels.0: Start and end times are recorded but the elapsed time is missing or equals one of those times.
levels.1: Aided by a clock face from the educator, elapsed time is found for whole hours only.
levels.2: Start and end times are noted for the task, and the length is worked out correctly in minutes or hours.
levels.3: Times a second, different task, compares the two lengths and explains how the answer was found from the clock.

rows.name: Project: 100 square
steps: Open the project '100 square' (unit 10) and give each child a hundred square.
Show a number pattern on the square with the first few terms marked, and ask what comes next.
Children continue the pattern on their square for three more terms, colouring each one.
Partners check each other's pattern and say the rule they followed.

levels.0: Coloured or marked squares show no regular rule, and the pattern is not extended.
levels.1: When the educator names the jump size, two more numbers are added before the pattern breaks.
levels.2: Three more numbers continue the pattern from the first few given on the hundred square, following the same jump.
levels.3: Spots and states the rule on the grid and creates a new pattern on a hundred square with a different jump.

rows.name: Making circuits
steps: Ask children to find where we use electricity at home and at school, and list their ideas on the board.
Show a battery, a bulb and wires, and show how to handle them safely.
In small groups, children make circuits by connecting the battery, bulb and wires until the bulb lights.
Children draw the circuit that worked and tell the class what they changed to make it light.

levels.0: Bulb stays unlit because wires touch only one end of the battery or bulb, and the attempt is left there.
levels.1: Guided to the battery ends, the bulb lights with partner help but the arrangement cannot be repeated.
levels.2: Battery, bulb and wires are joined in a loop so the bulb lights, and the arrangement can be rebuilt on request.
levels.3: Explains in own words why the bulb goes out when one wire is lifted, and lights it again using a new arrangement.

rows.name: Samaaroh project: stitched decor
steps: Recall the stitching techniques taught so far and show samples of each.
In groups, decide what decor to make for the Samaaroh event and sketch it with a colour plan.
Children use stitching techniques to create the decor, with each child stitching a part.
Display the finished decor and let each group say which techniques they used.

levels.0: Stitching is begun but only loose practice stitches exist, with no finished decor item.
levels.1: Stitched in parts with educator help threading and knotting, the decor item is left unfinished or uneven.
levels.2: A finished decor item for the event shows the stitching or weaving techniques taught in class.
levels.3: Finished decor combines more than one technique with a planned colour scheme, and the maker explains the choices for the event.

rows.name: Paper sculpture
steps: Show how paper can be folded, rolled, curled and joined to rise off the table.
Give each child paper and let them try folds and curls to see what stands up.
Children make a paper sculpture, choosing their own form.
Display the sculptures and let each child describe how they made theirs.

levels.0: Paper is flat, only folded once or drawn on, and does not stand or rise from the table.
levels.1: Following the educator's demonstration of rolling or folding, a shape stands but collapses when touched.
levels.2: A paper form that stands by itself shows height, width and depth, made by folding, rolling or curling.
levels.3: Joins several paper pieces into a sculpture of own design and explains how each fold or curl was chosen.

rows.name: Clay and dough work
steps: Give each child a lump of clay or dough and let them squeeze, roll and pinch it freely.
Show how to make a ball, a coil and a flat piece, and how pieces are joined.
Children work with clay and dough to model a shape of their choice.
Children show the shape to a partner and say what it is and how they made it.

levels.0: Material is pressed into a flat lump or left unshaped, with no recognisable form.
levels.1: Shown how to roll and pinch, a basic ball or coil forms but does not become the intended shape.
levels.2: A chosen shape is modelled with its main parts recognisable to a partner.
levels.3: Models a second, more detailed shape with added features and describes the steps used to build it.

rows.name: Portfolio building
steps: Give each child their folder of artwork made so far and a portfolio folder or file.
Ask children to look through their work and choose pieces they are proud of.
Children build an art portfolio, arranging the selected pieces in an order they decide.
Children show the portfolio to a partner and say why they chose and ordered the pieces as they did.

levels.0: Artwork is gathered loosely or stuffed in together, with nothing chosen and no order.
levels.1: Educator suggestions lead to a few pieces picked and placed in the folder without a plan for order.
levels.2: Chosen pieces sit in a folder in a planned order, each one placed on purpose.
levels.3: Explains why each piece was chosen and how the order was decided, and swaps one piece after a partner's feedback.

rows.name: Precise algorithms: draw a square from shouted instructions
steps: Tell the group that the educator will draw a square on the board only from instructions they shout out.
The educator tries to draw a square on the board from the shouted instructions; if they say 'Draw a line', draw a messy squiggle, and if they say 'Turn', turn around in a circle.
Explain that precise algorithms need clear distances and specific rotations.
In pairs, children write ordered steps for drawing a square with a distance and a turn in each, then swap and read them.

levels.0: Instructions are vague words like 'go' or 'turn' with no distances, so the drawn path would not form a square.
levels.1: Acting out the first lines with the educator, two or three steps come in order but turn size is missing.
levels.2: Written steps for drawing a square come in the right order, each with a distance or turn named.
levels.3: Tests the written steps on a partner and rewrites a vague step so the shape comes out right.

rows.name: ScratchJr: movement sequence across a grid of stepping stones
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open, and give each child a grid of stepping stones with water tiles marked.
In the tech log, children draw a path through the grid and write the numbers needed to cross it safely.
Children create an exact movement sequence for an animal sprite to reach a specific item across the grid without stepping on water tiles, using exact grid steps, e.g. Move Right 6, Move Down 2.
Run the program, check it against the drawn path, and share the sequence with a partner.

levels.0: Path blocks are placed at random, so the sprite lands on water tiles or never reaches the item.
levels.1: Counting squares aloud with a partner, the first moves are exact but the sprite stops short or enters water.
levels.2: Block sequence with exact numbers, such as Move Right 6, takes the sprite to the item avoiding water tiles.
levels.3: Finds a second, shorter route, writes its steps in the tech log, and explains why it avoids the water.

rows.name: Grade 2 worksheet: pick the correct precise command set from a map
steps: Hand out the worksheet and let children look at the map layout.
Ask children to trace the route on the map with a finger from start to finish.
Children select the correct precise command set from the multiple-choice list.
Partners compare choices and explain what was wrong with any option they rejected.

levels.0: Chosen command set sends the path through wrong squares, and the choice cannot be linked to the map route.
levels.1: Tracing the route with a finger beside the educator, the right set is picked for the shortest map only.
levels.2: On each map, the command set that matches the route in right order and distances is selected.
levels.3: Points out where a wrong option leaves the route and edits its steps so it fits the map.

rows.name: Human Keyboard game
steps: Explain that a clap or stomp is an input, and what the room does back is an output.
When the educator claps once (input), the room shouts 'Beep!' (output).
When the educator stomps a foot (input), the room jumps up (output).
Let children take turns giving the input, then ask the class to name the input and the output each time.

levels.0: In the game, the room responds to the wrong signal or cannot say which action was the signal and which the response.
levels.1: Pointing to the clap or stomp with the educator's help, signal and response are named for one round.
levels.2: Both rounds are described with a clear signal as input and a response as output, such as stomp then jump.
levels.3: Invents a new input and output pair for the game and links it to a device shown in a picture.

rows.name: ScratchJr: Start on Tap trigger
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open and talk about real-world inputs such as touching a screen.
In the tech log, children identify real-world inputs and draw a tablet screen being tapped by a finger.
Children build a program with the Start on Tap trigger block, coding a sprite to stay still until tapped, then spin or grow.
Children tap their sprite for a partner and name the input and the output.

levels.0: Sprite moves at once or not at all when tapped, and the tablet drawing shows no finger input or screen output.
levels.1: Shown the trigger block by a partner, the sprite starts on tap but the tap is not named as input.
levels.2: Tapping the sprite makes it spin or grow, and the tap is named as input and the change as output.
levels.3: Adds a second tap action and explains, using a picture of another device, what its input and output are.

rows.name: Colour the inputs blue and the outputs orange
steps: Hand out the worksheet and colours, and remind children that inputs go in and outputs come out.
Children colour the key-press input options blue.
Children colour the screen-output visuals orange.
Partners compare sheets and talk about any picture they coloured differently.

levels.0: Colours are mixed up, with key presses coloured orange or screen pictures coloured blue, or items left uncoloured.
levels.1: Starting from the first item named by the educator, blue and orange fit about half the pictures.
levels.2: All key-press options are coloured blue and all screen visuals orange, matching input and output.
levels.3: Gives own device example and says which part is coloured blue and which orange, with a reason.

rows.name: Paper flipbook animation
steps: Prepare a simple 3-page paper flipbook of a stick figure waving its arm.
Show the pages one at a time so children see the arm in a different place on each.
Flip the pages quickly to show how changing frames creates the illusion of life.
Children say what changed from page to page, and try the flipbook themselves.

levels.0: Describes the flipbook as one picture or says nothing changes between pages, with no mention of frames.
levels.1: Flipping slowly alongside the educator, one change between two pages, such as arm position, is named.
levels.2: Explains that each page shows a slightly different arm and quick flipping makes the figure appear to wave.
levels.3: Draws own three-frame flip and links it to a sprite changing its look when something happens on screen.

rows.name: ScratchJr Animal Animation
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open and pencils for the tech log.
In the tech log, children draw an animal sprite in two slightly different poses.
Children add a bird or frog sprite with multiple costume frames and choose a backdrop.
Children program a sequence that keeps changing the costume so it looks like flying or hopping across the backdrop, then show a partner.

levels.0: Sprite stays in one pose or jumps without changing costume, so no flying or hopping effect appears across the backdrop.
levels.1: Partner help adding costumes lets the sprite swap between two poses once without repeating.
levels.2: Sprite's costume frames change in sequence as it travels across the backdrop, so it looks like flying or hopping.
levels.3: Adds a start event such as a tap and adjusts frame timing, explaining which blocks give a smoother hop.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: Trace the sequence of animal costume frames
steps: Hand out the worksheet showing different animal costume frames.
Ask children to think which frame would come first and which next so the animal seems to move.
Children trace the line that connects different animal costume frames in logical order.
Partners compare traced lines and explain why they put the frames in that order.

levels.0: Traced line joins frames in a jumbled order, skips frames, or stops after one picture.
levels.1: Given the first frame by the educator, the line joins two or three frames in order before going wrong.
levels.2: The traced line joins all costume frames in the order that makes the animal appear to move.
levels.3: Explains why frames must run in that order and rearranges a mixed set of new frames correctly.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: Loops: five jumping jacks
steps: Ask the class to do 5 jumping jacks, counting aloud.
Write two code lists on the board: 'Jumping Jack' written 5 times, and Repeat 5 Times: [Jumping Jack].
Ask which option saves the most time and board space.
Children turn to a partner and give one more action they could write with Repeat instead of writing it out.

levels.0: Both code lists are said to be the same length, or the shorter one is not recognised as giving the same actions.
levels.1: Counting lines aloud with the educator, the Repeat 5 version is picked as shorter but no reason is given.
levels.2: Compares the five-line list with Repeat 5 and says the repeat uses fewer lines for the same five jumping jacks.
levels.3: Rewrites a different repeated action, such as clapping seven times, using Repeat and says how many lines it saves.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: ScratchJr Repeat Loop block
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open and pencils for the tech log.
In the tech log, children draw the loop bracket icon with the number 3 inside.
Children place a Move Right and a Hop block inside the Repeat bracket and run it.
Children change the loop number and observe how the actions run, then tell a partner what changed.

levels.0: Move Right and Hop blocks are placed outside the Repeat bracket, or the loop number is left unchanged and unexplained.
levels.1: Snapping blocks inside the bracket with help, the loop runs but a changed number does not match the predicted count.
levels.2: Move Right and Hop sit inside Repeat, and changing the number changes how many times the sprite moves and hops.
levels.3: Replaces a long row of repeated blocks with a Repeat loop and states the same result with fewer blocks.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: Count the steps in a Repeat 3 loop
steps: Write 'Repeat 3: Move 2 steps' on the board and have a child act it out.
Hand out the worksheet and ask children to count the total steps a character moves if it runs Move 2 steps inside a Repeat 3 loop.
Children show their working, by drawing the hops or writing the sum.
Partners compare totals and explain how they counted.

levels.0: Answer given is 2 or 3, showing only one number from the loop was used.
levels.1: Seeing three hops drawn on a line by the educator, steps are counted one by one to reach the total.
levels.2: Total of 6 steps is found for Repeat 3 with Move 2, shown by repeated addition or multiplication.
levels.3: Works out the total for a new Repeat count or step size and writes the matching shorter program.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: Debug a maze script step by step
steps: Draw a maze with dead ends on the board, with a long messy script beside it containing two errors.
Children test the path step by step with a finger, following the script line by line.
Stop where the code loses track, and children suggest what each error is and how to fix it.
As a class, rewrite the script with fewer blocks that still reach the exit.

levels.0: Finger path does not follow the script line by line, so the two errors stay unfound.
levels.1: Stopping at each line with the educator, one error is spotted but the other stays in the rewrite.
levels.2: Both errors are found by tracing and the script is rewritten with fewer blocks that still reach the maze exit.
levels.3: Explains where the messy script wasted steps and writes a shorter, correct script for a new maze.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: ScratchJr: find the missing trigger in a broken script
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open and the pre-broken script ready.
In the tech log, children draw a broken block connection next to a properly joined sequence.
Children load the pre-broken script where an element fails to trigger on touch.
Children step through the script to find the missing trigger block and rebuild the connection, then show a partner it now works.

levels.0: Pre-broken script is run but the gap is not found, and blocks are added at random without testing the touch.
levels.1: Stepping through blocks one at a time with a partner, the gap is pointed to but the fix needs help.
levels.2: Stepping through the script locates the missing trigger block, and the rebuilt connection makes the element respond on touch.
levels.3: Describes why the script failed, then fixes a second broken script and trims blocks that repeat.

source.fortnight: Monthly Planner_Grades 2 to 4 (Google Doc, no cells)

rows.name: Circle the broken connector in a ScratchJr block series
steps: Hand out the worksheet showing series of ScratchJr blocks, and remind children that blocks join like puzzle pieces.
Ask children to check each connector in a series, one join at a time, from the first block.
Children circle the broken puzzle connector link in each series of ScratchJr blocks.
Partners compare circles and explain how they knew that join was broken.

levels.0: Circles fall on whole blocks or intact joins, and the broken connector in the series stays unmarked.
levels.1: Tracing the first joins with the educator, the broken connector is circled in the shortest series only.
levels.2: Circle lands exactly on the broken puzzle connector in each series of ScratchJr blocks.
levels.3: Says what would happen when the script runs with the break, and draws the repaired join.

rows.name: Plus/Delta feedback on projects
steps: Discuss how to share constructive feedback politely, and write some sentence starters on the board.
Explain the Plus/Delta system: one thing that works well and one specific suggestion.
Model Plus/Delta together on one example project so children hear a good point and a polite suggestion.
Children give a classmate Plus/Delta feedback on their project, aloud or on a note.

rows.name: ScratchJr interactive habitat scene
steps: Hand out tablets with ScratchJr open and pencils for the tech log.
In the tech log, children draw a blueprint sketch of the final scene with background layout and character positions.
Children build an interactive habitat scene with at least two animal sprites.
Children use motion controls, sound effects and loop sequences when the sprites are clicked, then show the scene to a partner.

levels.0: Scene has backdrop and sprites but nothing happens when they are tapped.
levels.1: Adding triggers with a partner, one sprite moves when tapped while the second stays still.
levels.2: Both animal sprites respond to taps with motion, sound or a repeat loop, as sketched in the blueprint.
levels.3: Adds a chain of reactions, such as one tap starting both animals, and explains each block.

rows.name: Peer review loop
steps: Ask children to finish their projects and leave them open at their seats.
Students rotate chairs to test and explore projects built by classmates.
Each writes one feature they enjoyed in a classmate's project and one new coding concept they want to explore next term.
Share some notes in the circle so builders hear what classmates enjoyed.
